cards.front: A {{c1::circadian rhythm}} is a pattern in a living thing that repeats about every 24 hours.
cards.back: Example: sleepiness at night.
cards.quote: A circadian rhythm is a pattern in a living thing that repeats about every 24 hours, like your sleepiness at night.
cards.section: Explain: one day at a time

cards.front: What is a tropism?
cards.back: Growth of a plant toward or away from something in its surroundings, such as light or water.
cards.quote: A tropism is different: growth of a plant toward or away from something in its surroundings.
cards.section: Explain: one day at a time

cards.front: Do plants have daily rhythms? Give an example.
cards.back: Yes. Many plants have their own daily clock. Bean leaves lift during the day and droop at night.
cards.quote: Plants keep time too. Many have their own daily clock: bean leaves lift during the day and droop at night.
cards.section: Explain: one day at a time

cards.front: Why does a plant's bend toward light or water take from about half an hour to days to show?
cards.back: The bend is made of new growth, so it builds up slowly.
cards.quote: The bend is made of new growth, so it builds up slowly, from about half an hour to days.
cards.section: Explain: one day at a time

cards.front: A bean shoot has bent toward a lamp. The lamp is moved to the other side. Will the old bend flip, or will new growth change the shoot's direction?
cards.back: New growth changes the direction. The part that has stopped growing keeps its old bend. In the growing part, cells on the newly shaded side lengthen more, so new growth curves toward the lamp.
cards.quote: The part of the stem that has stopped growing keeps its old bend.
cards.section: Explain: one day at a time

cards.front: In lab tests, young roots in a dish bent toward the wetter side. Is this a circadian rhythm or a tropism, and why?
cards.back: A tropism. It is plant growth toward something in its surroundings (water), not a pattern that repeats about every 24 hours.
cards.quote: In lab tests, young roots bent toward the wetter side of their dish.
cards.section: Explain: one day at a time

cards.front: {{c1::Migration}} is the seasonal movement of animals from one region to another and back.
cards.back: Example: monarchs fly south in fall.
cards.quote: Migration is the seasonal movement of animals from one region to another and back.

cards.front: What is dormancy?
cards.back: A resting state in which a living thing slows or stops growing but stays alive until conditions improve.
cards.quote: Dormancy is a resting state in which a living thing slows or stops growing but stays alive until conditions improve.

cards.front: How is hibernation related to dormancy, and how does it help a groundhog through winter?
cards.back: Hibernation is dormancy in animals. Body temperature drops and the heart and breathing slow, so the groundhog uses less of its stored fat.
cards.quote: Body temperature drops and the heart and breathing slow, so a groundhog uses less of its stored fat.

cards.front: As days get shorter and the air cools, what makes a deciduous tree's leaf fall: cells in the leaf blade shrinking, or cells in a band at the leaf stalk coming apart?
cards.back: The cells in the band at the stalk come apart. This weakens the joint and the leaf falls. A protective layer then seals the scar.
cards.quote: The cells in the band start to come apart.

cards.front: How does dropping its leaves help a deciduous tree in winter?
cards.back: The tree loses less water. Frozen soil makes water hard to get in winter.
cards.quote: Without leaves, the tree loses less water in winter, when frozen soil makes water hard to get.

cards.front: Behaviors an animal inherits and can do without being taught are called {{c1::instincts}}.
cards.quote: Many of the animal behaviors here are instincts: behaviors an animal inherits and can do without being taught.

cards.front: A monarch hatched in Virginia in August flies toward Mexico in the fall. It has never made this trip. What best explains its behavior?
cards.back: An inherited instinct to fly south in fall. A first trip south does not need to be taught.
cards.quote: Many seasonal behaviors of animals, such as a monarch's first trip south, are inherited instincts.

cards.front: Groundhogs were kept in rooms where day length never changed. Their eating and weight-gain cycles kept repeating about once a year for up to 4 years. What does this show?
cards.back: Groundhogs have an inner yearly clock. The timing does not depend only on outside cues.
cards.quote: In rooms where the day length never changed, their cycles of eating and weight gain kept repeating about once a year for up to 4 years.

cards.front: Young aspen trees got 10 weeks of short, 8-hour days, then 5 weeks at 4 °C, then warm long days. Their buds swelled and leaves came out. What does the sequence show about how buds time spring opening?
cards.back: Short days put the buds into dormancy, and the sequence is consistent with cold then readying them to open in warmth. It rests on the rule that many buds need enough winter cold before later warmth can open them.
cards.quote: In a 2018 experiment, young aspen trees got 10 weeks of short, 8-hour days, and their buds went dormant.

cards.front: A winter is too warm to give a tree's buds enough cold. What may happen to the buds in spring?
cards.back: Some buds may open late or unevenly. Many buds need enough winter cold before later warmth can open them.
cards.quote: If a winter is too warm to give enough cold, some buds may open late or unevenly.
cards.section: Explain: when the long-term pattern shifts

cards.front: In the Tidal Basin cherry record, what does peak bloom mean?
cards.back: The day when about 70 percent of the Yoshino cherry blossoms around the Tidal Basin are open.
cards.quote: Peak bloom is the day when about 70 percent of the Yoshino cherry blossoms around the Tidal Basin are open.
cards.section: Elaborate: a century of cherry blossoms

cards.front: Day 91 is April 1 in a year that is not a leap year. The mean peak-bloom day for 1960 to 1969 was 97.4. About which date is that?
cards.back: 97.4 - 91 = 6.4, so about 6 days after April 1, which is about April 7.
cards.quote: Each date is a day of the year: January 1 is day 1, and day 91 is April 1 in a year that is not a leap year.
cards.section: Elaborate: a century of cherry blossoms

cards.front: The Tidal Basin mean peak-bloom day was 97.4 for 1960 to 1969 and 90.9 for 1990 to 1999. Which decade was earlier, and by how many days?
cards.back: 1990 to 1999 was earlier, by 97.4 - 90.9 = 6.5 days. A smaller day number is earlier in the year.
cards.quote: The Tidal Basin record shows the mean bloom date moving earlier after the 1960s, though not in a steady line.

cards.front: In the Tidal Basin record, the mean peak-bloom day was 93.4 for 1940 to 1949 and 96.8 for 1950 to 1959. Did the mean get earlier in every decade?
cards.back: No. It got later by 96.8 - 93.4 = 3.4 days. The record moves earlier overall after the 1960s, though not in a steady line.
cards.quote: The Tidal Basin record shows the mean bloom date moving earlier after the 1960s, though not in a steady line.

cards.front: A student says the cherry bloom record proves that warming made the trees bloom earlier. What is a fair reply?
cards.back: The dates show a pattern, but they alone cannot prove what caused it. A claim needs evidence and reasoning, and the record shows only the timing.
cards.quote: The dates show a pattern, but they alone cannot prove what caused it.

cards.front: A test asks whether bean seedlings bend toward light from one side. Some boxes have a hole on one side and others a hole on top. Which are the control seedlings, and what should they do?
cards.back: The top-lit seedlings. Their stems should grow straight up, which gives a comparison for the side-lit stems.
cards.quote: Control: seedlings in boxes lit from the top. Their stems should grow straight up.

cards.front: Plan a test of whether young roots grow toward wetter soil. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and one constant, using the bean-light test as your model.
cards.back: Independent: which side of the dish is wetter. Dependent: how far each root bends toward the wetter side, measured as in the bean test. Constant: same kind of seed, soil, dish and room. Repeat the trial several times.
cards.quote: Dependent variable: the angle of each stem from straight up, in degrees, measured with a protractor after 5 days.

cards.front: How has a warming climate changed where many land species live?
cards.back: Many now live farther toward the poles or higher up mountains than before.
cards.quote: As the climate has warmed, many land species now live farther toward the poles or higher up mountains than before.
